text: Project documentsArchitecture Code

Overview
The analysis is a set of R scripts that run in sequence in one R session. R/main.R is the only entry point. It sources:

a setup script (libraries, constants, code lists)
a cohort-construction script
a figures script

All USRDS file access goes through the usRds package. Cohort inclusions and exclusions are recorded with the flowchart package, so the participant flowchart is produced directly from the cohort-building code.
Every object lives in the global environment of the session. The pipeline writes nothing to disk: no intermediate files, and no exported tables or figures. Restricted data are read from the USRDS data directory configured for usRds and stay in memory.
Current scope. The code builds a cohort of kidney transplant recipients with a cryptococcosis claim and draws its flowchart. Not yet implemented:

the missed-opportunity algorithm
comorbidities
mortality and geographic analyses
any Quarto documents
Architecture diagram

Data flow











transplant_df, facility, and transplant_joined are built, but they are not yet joined to the cohort. They are dead ends in the current flow.
How the cohort moves through create_cohort.R:

Base population. Load the USRDS patient file, dropping the ZIP code recorded when the patient entered USRDS. Wrap it in a flowchart object, then keep patients with at least one transplant.
Case finding. Collect the IDs of the patients still in the cohort. Pull institutional and physician/supplier claims that carry a code from the cryptococcosis list, for the claim years in the constants. Combine the two sources, then keep each patient’s earliest claim date as first_cryptococcus_date.
Attach and filter. Join that date to the flowchart’s data with a one-to-one join. Then apply two flowchart filters: the patient has a claim, and the claim falls after the first transplant date.
Medicare coverage. verify_medicare_primary() adds the start and end dates of the Medicare primary coverage span that contains the index date, plus a TRUE/FALSE flag for whether that span covers the look-back period. A duplicate check stops the run if the join multiplied rows. Two flowchart filters then apply the coverage criteria.
Residence. An interval join adds the ZIP code valid on the index date, followed by a duplicate check. Patients with no matching residence period are kept, with a missing ZIP code.
Transplant and facility (not connected). Builds a per-transplant table with the date of the next transplant (a far-future placeholder when there is none), and joins each transplant to facility records by provider and year.

figures.R then draws the flowchart from the final patients_fc.

Components

Entry point
Purpose: runs the full pipeline in dependency order.
Location: R/main.R
Interactions: sources R/setup.R, R/create_cohort.R, and R/figures.R, in that order, from the project root.


Setup
Purpose: loads every library, and defines the constants and code lists that the other scripts use.
Location: R/setup.R
Labelled sections: libraries, constants, icd-code-lists, missed-diagnosis-code-maps
Key objects:

claim_years: the claim years searched
lookback_days: the days of Medicare primary coverage required before the index date
icd10_start_date: the date ICD-10 coding begins (defined but not used yet)
cryptococcus_ICD_list: the ICD-9 and ICD-10 case-finding codes, matched exactly
icd9_map, icd10_map, and icd_combined_map: symptom, condition, and procedure codes for possible earlier presentations, by category and code type (not used yet)

Interactions: provides constants and code lists to create_cohort.R. Nothing upstream.


Cohort construction
Purpose: builds the analytic cohort and records each inclusion step in the flowchart.
Location: R/create_cohort.R
Labelled sections: load-usrds-files, initialize-flowchart, cryptococcus-claims, develop-flowchart, medicare-coverage, residence-transplant-facility
Key objects:

patients_fc: the flowchart object. Its $data element is the cohort, one row per patient.
cryptococcus_claims_df: every cryptococcosis claim for transplant recipients, from both claim sources
cryptococcus_df: the earliest cryptococcosis claim date per patient
ZIP_code_df: residence periods
transplant_df, facility, and transplant_joined: transplant and facility tables, not yet used downstream

External functions:

usRds: load_usrds_file(), get_IN_ICD(), get_PS_ICD(), verify_medicare_primary()
flowchart: as_fc(), fc_filter()

Interactions: takes constants and code lists from setup, and reads the USRDS files through usRds. Passes patients_fc to figures.


Figures
Purpose: draws the participant flowchart.
Location: R/figures.R
Labelled sections: final-flowchart
External functions: flowchart’s fc_draw()
Interactions: takes patients_fc from cohort construction. The diagram is drawn in the session and not exported.

External dependencies







Dependency
Role




usRds
Locates and reads USRDS files; extracts claims by ICD code; checks Medicare primary coverage. All data access goes through it.


flowchart
Records cohort filtering steps and draws the participant flowchart


tidyverse, lubridate
Data manipulation and dates


USRDS data directory
The restricted source files, outside the repository. Its location is set through usRds outside this code; no script sets it.

Configuration

Analysis constants: in R/setup.R (see Setup above). Flowchart labels in create_cohort.R still hard-code the claim years and the 365-day look-back, so they do not follow the constants.
Data location: set through usRds’s own configuration, not in this repository.
Ignored files: .gitignore covers RStudio and session files (.Rproj.user, .Rhistory, .Rdata), .DS_Store, .httr-oauth, and .quarto.

Chunk labels
Each script is divided into sections marked ## ---- label, so that Quarto documents can load them with knitr::read_chunk(). The labels in each script are listed under Components above. No Quarto documents exist yet. README.Rmd is the unedited usethis template, and it renders README.md together with an example figure in README_files/.

Glossary







Term
Meaning in this repository




IN claims
USRDS institutional claims: inpatient, outpatient, SNF, home health, and hospice. Not inpatient only.


PS claims
USRDS physician/supplier claims


HCFASAF
The claim-type variable on claims returned by usRds


Index date
Currently first_cryptococcus_date, the earliest cryptococcosis claim of any type. analysis-plan.md defines the intended index date.


patients_fc
The flowchart object. patients_fc$data is the cohort, and its filter history becomes the flowchart.


Look-back
The days of continuous Medicare primary coverage required before the index date (lookback_days)

title: Setup
text: This script attaches the packages and defines the constants and code lists that every other script uses. R/main.R sources it first.

title: Setup
text:
Libraries
The analysis uses the tidyverse and lubridate for data management and dates, usRds to load USRDS files and extract Medicare claims, and flowchart to build the cohort so that the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. These are the only library() calls in the project; other scripts rely on them.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Data management libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

#Core library for the USRDS
library(usRds)

#Flowchart library
library(flowchart)

title: Setup
text:
Constants
Numbers a reader might want to change live here as named constants, so downstream scripts and flowchart labels use one definition:

claim_years: the calendar years of institutional (IN) and physician/supplier (PS) claims searched for cryptococcosis.
lookback_days: the days of Medicare primary coverage required before the first cryptococcosis claim.
icd10_start_date: the ICD-9-CM to ICD-10 transition date. It is defined but not yet used by any script.

The plan sets index-date eligibility from the date range in which claims are complete for the release analyzed (analysis plan, section 2); claim_years is the current code’s fixed range.


Click to show/hide R Code
claim_years <- 2006:2021                   #Years of IN and PS claims searched
lookback_days <- 365                       #Days of Medicare primary coverage required before the first cryptococcus claim
icd10_start_date <- as.Date("2015-10-01")  #ICD-9-CM before this date, ICD-10-CM/PCS on or after

title: Setup
text:
Cryptococcosis codes
cryptococcus_ICD_list holds the ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes for cryptococcosis, stored without periods. The usRds claim functions match them exactly. Section 3 of the analysis plan calls for a clinically reviewed list.


Click to show/hide R Code
#ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes for cryptococcus (matched exactly by get_IN_ICD and get_PS_ICD)
cryptococcus_ICD_list <- c("1175", "3210", "B450", "B451", "B452", "B453", "B457", "B458", "B459")

title: Setup
text:
Missed-opportunity code maps
icd9_map and icd10_map list the diagnosis and procedure codes for the categories that could signal an earlier presentation of cryptococcosis: lumbar puncture, increased intracranial pressure, brain infection, encephalopathy, headache, focal neurological deficit, stroke, pneumonia, pleural and mediastinal disease, signs of infection, and infection not otherwise specified. Each row records the category, whether the code is a diagnosis or a procedure, and the code. icd_combined_map stacks the two. No script uses the maps yet; they are the starting point for the opportunity ascertainment in sections 5 and 6 of the plan, which requires clinically reviewed, era-appropriate exact or prefix rules.

title: About
text:
This study asks how often kidney transplant recipients with cryptococcosis had earlier health care encounters that may have been missed opportunities for diagnosis. The analysis is preliminary: the analysis plan is a proposal not yet adopted, and no results have been released.

Vagish Hemmige
Hyun ah Yoon

Vagish Hemmige and Hyun ah Yoon make the scientific decisions. Open decisions are listed in GitHub Issues.

title: About
text:
This repository
R/main.R runs the scripts in order: setup, cohort construction, and figures. The data come from the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), including its linked Medicare claims, loaded through the usRds package. USRDS data are restricted under a data use agreement, so they are not in the repository; the code runs only where an authorized person has access to them.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; known issues and open decisions are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the analysis data. A GitHub Actions workflow renders and publishes it whenever master changes.
The repository follows the R Analysis Workflow plugin and the layout of Cryptococcus-cost-analysis. AI assistants may help draft and review code and documentation. They never see the USRDS data, they work on synthetic data only, and every change reaches master only through a pull request a person reviews and merges.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why. The question, the population, the methods, and the open decisions. Code implements it and does not redefine it.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project. Rules for restricted data, coding, checks, proposing changes and getting a person’s approval.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from, which the architecture document then describes as built.

title: About
text:
Pages

Setup: packages, shared constants, and the cryptococcosis and missed-opportunity code lists.
1. Create cohort: builds the cohort through the flowchart and attaches residence and transplant-center information.
Figures: draws the cohort flow diagram.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: Overview
text: This analysis looks for potential missed opportunities to diagnose cryptococcosis among kidney transplant recipients in the United States. It uses the United States Renal Data System (USRDS) and its linked Medicare fee-for-service claims to find health care encounters, in the 90 days before a recipient’s first observed qualifying cryptococcosis diagnosis, that carried a relevant diagnosis or diagnostic procedure. These are claims-based potential missed opportunities, not confirmed diagnostic errors.

text:
Methods
The primary estimand is the proportion of eligible recipients with at least one qualifying encounter in days −90 through −1, reported separately for diagnosis-based, procedure-based, and combined opportunities, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals1. Secondary analyses examine associations with mortality, rurality, and distance to the transplant center. Reporting follows STROBE and RECORD2,3. The analysis plan is the authoritative specification.

title: Overview
text:
Status
This analysis is preliminary. The analysis plan is a proposal that has not yet been adopted, and the code currently builds the initial cohort only. Open decisions and known gaps are tracked in GitHub Issues.

Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This is an R analysis project, not an R package. It examines potential missed opportunities to diagnose cryptococcosis among kidney transplant recipients using USRDS and Medicare claims. The code and methods are published as a Quarto website. Do not introduce package infrastructure or impose CRAN conventions.

The analysis plan is the scientific source of truth. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If implementation needs a different design, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue. Track decisions in Git history and issues rather than a change ledger within the plan.
Deciders. Scientific decisions in every area are made by Vagish Hemmige and Hyun ah Yoon. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Do not make unresolved scientific decisions implicitly through code. Check relevant open GitHub issues before implementing analyses that depend on them.
Maintain implementation status and defects in GitHub Issues rather than in a standing list inside this file.
Default branch: master. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources
Each source this project uses is listed below with the package that accesses it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. Do not write project-specific loading, cleaning, or definition code for something the package already does.











Source
Accessed through
Package documentation
Package maintained by

What AI agents may do

usRds (load_usrds_file(), get_IN_ICD(), get_PS_ICD())
https://vagishhemmige.github.io/usRds/
This team
Restricted (USRDS data use agreement)
None: code, documentation and synthetic data only



To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
Add a row when code first loads a new source (for example, the USDA ZIP-code RUCA file the plan’s geographic analyses use).
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains: see “Look in usRds first” below.
For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

For a source with no package: one loading script records the download URL, the release or access date, and any processing. Verify its variables against the provider’s documentation for that release.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Open the .Rproj and run R/main.R from the project root. main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Keep scripts focused on one analytical responsibility. Study-specific scripts may be grouped in stage-specific subdirectories. Include a short header stating the script’s role, its required upstream objects, and what it produces.
When a definitive script is added or structurally reorganized, source it in main.R as appropriate and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request when the change materially affects structure or data flow. ARCHITECTURE.md describes current implementation, not planned work.
Define shared libraries, paths, configurable analytical constants, and their dependencies in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code study parameters. Large, version-controlled code lists may live in separate files sourced by setup.R.
Place reusable helpers in R/functions.R, or organized subdirectories when warranted. Prefer explicit function arguments over dependence on global objects.
Avoid setwd(), machine-specific absolute paths, and writes outside designated project outputs. Locate restricted USRDS inputs through usRds’s directory configuration.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from restricted data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto can reuse code without copying it:
## ---- cryptococcus-claims

Label logical steps with descriptive kebab-case identifiers unique across scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code. A label covers code up to the next label.
Before renaming or removing a label, check the .qmd pages that reference it.
Labels are comments; the underlying R scripts must remain executable through main.R.

Variable labels

Label analytical variables with human-readable descriptions (for example, labelled::set_variable_labels()).
For USRDS fields, prefer usRds::apply_usrds_varlabels() and usRds::apply_usrds_factors() rather than duplicating source labels.
Label derived variables where created, including units and time windows where relevant.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis. Exploratory scripts need no page.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it (for example, quarto/create_cohort.qmd for R/create_cohort.R), plus the Background, Study design and methods, About and project-document pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, link the decision issue, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each script page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why, without duplicating source code. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages that read cleared outputs run. Review any proposed publication of aggregate results separately for disclosure compliance.
Publishing. The site renders to docs/, which is not committed: a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) renders it on every push to master and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. On a pull request the workflow only renders, as a check that every page builds.
When you add a definitive script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request. Prose must match the code: if a change alters what a section does, or its chunk labels, update its explanation and navigation in the same pull request.

Outputs

R/tables.R and R/figures.R may create outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts, exporting to tables/ and figures/.
tables/ and figures/ are gitignored until USRDS review before publication clears them for release, because they come from restricted data: agents may not open them (see Restricted data). Commit cleared, nonrestricted results only when intentional. Disclosure rules apply to all outputs.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
USRDS and Medicare data are governed by a data use agreement (DUA). Applicable DUA requirements take precedence over convenience or automation. The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, person-level data objects, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep restricted source data outside the repository, and review output paths and .gitignore before adding new output types.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers (including USRDS IDs), person-level dates, or ZIP codes. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person in an authorized environment. A request to execute a pipeline does not itself provide authorization. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. Prevent disclosure of counts 1–10 in tables, figures, flowcharts, or prose, including counts recoverable by subtraction or complementary cells. Follow the applicable DUA’s exact dissemination rules. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls.

Look in usRds first
The usRds package is the first place to look for USRDS file loading, claims extraction, claim types, diagnosis dates, Medicare coverage, cohort helpers, and costs.

Check its documentation, known limitations, and open issues before reproducing functionality locally.
Raise generally reusable defects or enhancements in usRds; prefer fixes there. Temporary project-specific wrappers must identify the upstream issue and be reconsidered when resolved.
When this analysis depends on a pending usRds enhancement or correction, track the study-specific implementation task here and link it to the corresponding usRds issue.
Record the usRds version or commit used for any result.

USRDS data facts
Sources: the Researcher’s Guide, Appendix B, and Appendix C for the specific USRDS release being analyzed. The summary below is a starting point, not a replacement for release-appropriate documentation. Obtain the applicable public documents from the NIDDK Researcher’s Guide page. Consult usRds for machine-readable variable labels and formats.
Institutional (IN) claims include inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing facility, home health, and hospice services.

HCFASAF historically distinguishes I inpatient, O outpatient, N SNF, H home health, and S hospice; older data can include M for REBUS inpatient stays.
Since 2002, corresponding file families include ip_*, op_*, sn_*, hh_*, and hs_*, generally with CLM, DXP, and DET records. Confirm structure for the release.
Institutional claim identifiers include USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, and SEQ_KEYC; verify the applicable key in source documentation.

Physician/supplier (PS) claims have CLM, LINE, and DX sources.

Claim lines are not necessarily distinct encounters. Define and validate episode grouping before counting services; distinguish diagnoses, procedures, and claim-level versus line-level records.
Physician/supplier services are not synonymous with outpatient care.

Claims year: claims can be assigned by service end date rather than start date; verify against release documentation and account for claims crossing year boundaries.
2025-release data currency (illustrative only; re-verify for the release used): claims complete through 2023-12-31 except the Q1 2024 inpatient file; core files including death dates extend through 2024-12-31. Do not infer contemporaneous coverage of claims and vital status.
Payer history (payhist): payer categories and Medicare FFS observability must be verified against the release-specific guide. The primary versus sensitivity coverage definitions are prescribed in analysis-plan.md, not here. Pay attention to Medicare Advantage, Medicare secondary payer categories, uncovered days, and Medicare entitlement transitions after transplantation.
ICD transition: ICD-9-CM applies before 2015-10-01; ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS on or after that date. Codes may omit decimals. Establish the date controlling the code system for claims spanning the transition, and verify against official code-set definitions.
Unclear variables: consult the relevant Appendix B/C and source code documentation rather than inferring meaning from variable names.

Coding conventions

Build descriptive flowchart text from centrally defined parameters so labels cannot become stale when an analysis window changes.
Code lists: maintain code type, coding system, category, and exact/prefix matching; verify against official coding sources. Distinguish outcome from opportunity codes and personal-history from symptom codes. Do not invent clinical definitions or variables. Check category overlaps and clinically justified exceptions rather than assuming all codes are mutually exclusive.
Cohort flow: every patient-level inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter() in the flowchart workflow. Do not drop rows from $data outside the flowchart; the diagram must reproduce the cohort exactly.
Joins: specify join keys and expected relationships. Check row multiplication, particularly after interval joins, and define handling of missing or unmatched records explicitly.
Dates and windows: implement the boundaries prespecified in the analysis plan; test boundary cases on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory.
Style: use readable tidyverse conventions. Related readability improvements may accompany functional changes; keep unrelated large-scale formatting separate.

Checks for any change
Before presenting changes for review or seeking commit approval, perform the applicable checks below. Report which checks were completed, which were not, and any limitations.
Every change

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use usRds’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from restricted data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.

Cohort construction

Do the order, denominator, and labels of flowchart steps reflect the actual conditions?
Are the cohort counts reproducible from the operations shown?
Is downstream analysis based on the final flowchart dataset?

Claims and case definitions

Which claim files, claim types, diagnosis fields, and date fields are used?
Are exact/prefix matching and ICD-9/ICD-10 date transitions handled appropriately?
Can history codes, rule-out diagnoses, or outcome codes contaminate opportunities?

Windows and coverage

Does index ascertainment agree with the analysis plan?
Are date-window boundaries correct and inclusive where specified?
Does eligible Medicare coverage span the entire required observation period, with adjacent spans joined without allowing gaps?

Transplant timing

Are first and repeat transplants distinguished where the analysis requires them?
Are transplant dates and characteristics drawn from the correct episode according to the analysis plan?
Are graft failure and repeat transplants treated as prespecified?

Residence and facility

Is residence information valid for the relevant date?
Is facility information aligned to the appropriate year and transplant center?
Are historical identifiers and changes in identifiers accounted for?

Structure and documentation

Does ARCHITECTURE.md describe current scripts and data flow when structural changes warrant an update?
Are chunk labels unique, and do Quarto pages continue to find the labels they reference?
Does every definitive script have a Quarto page and sidebar entry, with matching chunk labels? Were affected pages and navigation updated?
Does any site chunk evaluate analysis code, and are derived variables labeled?

Execution

Does main.R run from a clean session, using suitable relative paths?
Are machine-specific absolute paths or hard-coded restricted-data directories absent?
Are package versions and saved intermediates documented and checked for staleness?

Validation on real data (by an authorized person only; share only permitted, disclosure-reviewed aggregate findings)

Row counts before and after interval joins.
Counts of people with multiple matching coverage or residence spans.
Case counts by ICD-9 versus ICD-10 era and by claim type.

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request. Explicit approval is required before committing changes or opening a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive external/API calls (approval for these does not override DUA restrictions); shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as clinical results.
Scientific citations: maintain verified references in root-level references.bib; cite methodological sources in analysis-plan.md and technical references with the corresponding implementation documentation. Verify bibliographic metadata, source support for claims, and compatibility with the data release being analyzed.

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
This script builds the cohort of kidney transplant recipients with a cryptococcosis claim after their first transplant and Medicare primary coverage before it, records each exclusion in a flowchart, and attaches residence and transplant-center information for later scripts.
Every inclusion and exclusion goes through fc_filter() from the flowchart package, so the cohort flow diagram drawn on the Figures page reproduces the cohort exactly. The cohort used downstream is patients_fc$data after the last step.

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
Load the patient file
The USRDS patients file supplies one row per person with demographics and transplant summary fields, loaded through usRds::load_usrds_file(). Its ZIP code is dropped here because it is the ZIP code when the person entered USRDS; the analysis needs residence at the time of the cryptococcosis claim, which is attached in the last step.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Import core demographics from "patients" file
patients_raw<-usRds::load_usrds_file("patients")%>%
  select(-ZIPCODE) #This is ZIP code at time of USRDS initiation, but we want at time of crypto dx

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
Start the flowchart
The patient file becomes a flowchart object, and the first step keeps people with at least one recorded transplant (TOTTX > 0).


Click to show/hide R Code
#Initialize a flowchart cohort and remove patients who have never had a transplant
patients_fc<-patients_raw%>%
  as_fc(label="Initial USRDS cohort")%>%

  fc_filter(TOTTX>0,
            label="Prior transplant",
            label_exc="Excluded: No prior transplant",
            show_exc=TRUE)

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
Find cryptococcosis claims
For the people still in the cohort, get_IN_ICD() and get_PS_ICD() from usRds search the institutional and physician/supplier claims of the years in claim_years for the codes in cryptococcus_ICD_list (see Setup). The two sets are stacked, and each person’s earliest claim of any type, by claim start date, is kept as first_cryptococcus_date.
Section 3 of the analysis plan specifies a confirmed case (one inpatient stay, or two noninpatient encounters no more than 30 days apart), an index date within the qualifying episode, a uniform prior-history exclusion, and excludes skilled nursing, home health and hospice claims from ascertainment (section 2). The current code uses the first single claim and does not yet apply those rules.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Create list of USRDS ids for patients who have undergone transplant
transplant_id_list<-patients_fc$data%>%
  pull(USRDS_ID)

#Obtain cryptococcus claims from the IN and PS files
cryptococcus_claims_df<-bind_rows(get_IN_ICD(icd_codes = cryptococcus_ICD_list,
                                             years = claim_years,
                                             usrds_ids = transplant_id_list),
                                  get_PS_ICD(icd_codes = cryptococcus_ICD_list,
                                             years = claim_years,
                                             usrds_ids = transplant_id_list)%>%
                                    rename(CODE=DIAG))

#Keep the first cryptococcus claim of any type for each patient
cryptococcus_df<-cryptococcus_claims_df%>%
  slice_min(CLM_FROM, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = USRDS_ID)%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, first_cryptococcus_date=CLM_FROM)

title: 1. Create cohort
section: Apply the claim and transplant-timing steps
text:
Apply the claim and transplant-timing steps
The first claim date is joined to the cohort one-to-one by USRDS_ID. Two flowchart steps follow: people with no cryptococcosis claim in the search years are excluded, and so are people whose first claim is not after their first transplant date (TX1DATE). The plan requires a kidney transplant strictly before the index date (section 4).


Click to show/hide R Code
#Join cryptococcus date to fc cohort (one row per patient on both sides)
patients_fc$data<-patients_fc$data%>%
  left_join(cryptococcus_df,
            by = "USRDS_ID",
            relationship = "one-to-one")

patients_fc<-patients_fc%>%

  #Filter by whether or not the patient had a claim in the study period
  fc_filter(!is.na(first_cryptococcus_date),
            label="At least one cryptococcus claim 2006-2021",
            label_exc="No cryptococcus claim 2006-2021",
            show_exc=TRUE)%>%

  #Filter by whether or not the first claim was subsequent to the first kidney transplant date
  fc_filter(first_cryptococcus_date>TX1DATE,
            label="Cryptococcus subsequent to first transplant",
            label_exc="Excluded: Cryptococcus prior to first transplant",
            show_exc=TRUE)

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
Apply the Medicare coverage steps
usRds::verify_medicare_primary() adds the Medicare primary coverage spell in force on the first claim date, if any, and medicare_primary_TF, which is true when that spell began at least lookback_days earlier. A check stops the script if the coverage join produced more than one row for anyone. Two flowchart steps then keep people with Medicare primary coverage on the claim date, and people with coverage for the full lookback.
The plan’s primary cohort requires uninterrupted Medicare fee-for-service Parts A and B (MPAB) coverage from day −365 through day 0, with broader primary coverage (MPAB or MPO) as a sensitivity analysis (section 4). Which payer categories count as primary here is set by verify_medicare_primary(); see the usRds documentation.


Click to show/hide R Code
#Mark Medicare FFS primary coverage on the date of the first cryptococcus claim, and whether
#that coverage spell began at least lookback_days earlier (adds medicare_primary_TF)
patients_fc$data<-patients_fc$data%>%
  verify_medicare_primary(index_date = "first_cryptococcus_date",
                          lookback_days = lookback_days,
                          coverage_start_variable = "coverage_start_date",
                          coverage_end_variable = "coverage_end_date")

#Confirm the coverage join did not duplicate patients
if (anyDuplicated(patients_fc$data$USRDS_ID) > 0) {
  stop("Medicare coverage join produced more than one row for some patients.")
}

patients_fc<-patients_fc%>%

  #Filter by Medicare primary coverage on day of claim
  fc_filter(!is.na(coverage_start_date),
            label="Medicare is primary coverage on date of claim",
            label_exc="Other coverage on date of claim",
            show_exc=TRUE)%>%

  #Filter by coverage for lookback_days before the claim
  fc_filter(medicare_primary_TF,
            label="365+ days of coverage prior to first cryptococcus claim",
            label_exc="Fewer than 365 days of coverage",
            show_exc=TRUE)

title: 1. Create cohort
text:
Attach residence and transplant center
The residenc file is joined to the cohort by an interval join, keeping the residence spell that contains the first claim date, and a check stops the script if that join duplicated anyone. The tx file is loaded with each transplant’s date, graft failure date, and center, and each transplant gets the date of the person’s next transplant (a far-future date when there is none), ready for choosing the transplant episode that precedes the index date. The facility file supplies each center’s ZIP code by year, matched to each transplant by center and the closest facility year at or after the transplant year.
These transplant and facility tables (transplant_df, transplant_joined) are built but not yet joined to the cohort. The plan uses the most recent kidney transplant before index for transplant characteristics and center (section 4).


Click to show/hide R Code
#Load ZIP codes
ZIP_code_df<-load_usrds_file("residenc",
                             usrds_ids = patients_fc$data$USRDS_ID)%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, ZIPCODE, BEGRES, ENDRES)

#Join patient cohort to ZIP code at the date of the first cryptococcus claim
patients_fc$data<-left_join(patients_fc$data,
                            ZIP_code_df,
                            join_by(USRDS_ID, between(first_cryptococcus_date, BEGRES, ENDRES)))

#Confirm the residence join did not duplicate patients
if (anyDuplicated(patients_fc$data$USRDS_ID) > 0) {
  stop("Residence join produced more than one row for some patients.")
}

#Load transplant data, and add a date for the next transplant (missing set to 1-1-2100)
transplant_df<-load_usrds_file("tx", usrds_ids = patients_fc$data$USRDS_ID)%>%
  select(USRDS_ID, TDATE, FAILDATE, PROVUSRD, YEAR)%>%
  arrange(USRDS_ID, TDATE)%>%
  group_by(USRDS_ID)%>%
  mutate(TDATE_lead=lead(TDATE))%>%
  ungroup()%>%
  mutate(TDATE_lead=coalesce(TDATE_lead, as.Date("2100-01-01")))

#Load facility data
facility <- load_usrds_file("facility")%>%
  select(ZIPCODE, PROVUSRD, FS_YEAR)%>%
  rename(YEAR=FS_YEAR)%>%
  mutate(YEAR=as.double(YEAR))

#Interval merge
transplant_joined<-left_join(transplant_df, facility, join_by(PROVUSRD, closest(x$YEAR<=y$YEAR )))
Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands, and statistical methods. It describes what the analysis must accomplish, independently of how the code is organized or implemented. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation structure and data flow, while AGENTS.md provides instructions and conventions for working with the repository. Neither document supersedes scientific decisions in this analysis plan.
Reporting will follow STROBE and RECORD1,2.

1. Overview and aims
Building on the 90-day inpatient missed-opportunity approach of Salazar et al.3, this retrospective study uses USRDS data linked to Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) institutional and physician/supplier (PS) claims to identify claims-based potential missed opportunities, not confirmed diagnostic errors, before the first observed qualifying post-transplant cryptococcosis diagnosis.
Primary estimand: Proportion of eligible recipients with at least one qualifying encounter during days −90 through −1, reported for diagnosis-based, procedure-based, and combined opportunities, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals4.
Secondary objectives: Associations of any opportunity with 90-day all-cause mortality, and of (separately) ZIP-code RUCA rurality and continuous distance to the transplant center with any opportunity. Additional mortality horizons: 30 and 365 days. Graft outcomes are exploratory only if defensibly ascertained.
These are observational associations; they do not estimate the causal effect of delay.

2. Sources and observation
Use USRDS transplant, treatment, payer, patient, residence, facility and mortality records as applicable; use inpatient and outpatient institutional and PS claims for ascertainment. Institutional files can include inpatient, hospital outpatient, skilled nursing, home health and hospice services5. Skilled nursing facility, home health, and hospice claims are excluded from case and opportunity ascertainment under the prespecified study scope.
Determine index-date eligibility from the date range in which claims are complete and the full preceding 365-day eligibility window can be observed. Mortality ascertainment has its own end date and must not be equated to claims availability. Use documentation applicable to the actual SAF release5.
ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM coding eras are combined in the primary analysis, with separate era-specific sensitivity estimates. For the October 1, 2015 transition, outpatient/professional coding follows service date and hospital inpatient coding follows discharge date6.

3. Case ascertainment and index
Cryptococcosis is identified using clinically reviewed diagnosis codes in any qualifying diagnosis position. A confirmed case satisfies either: - one inpatient stay with a cryptococcosis code; or - two distinct noninpatient encounters (outpatient institutional or PS not belonging to the same inpatient stay), each with a cryptococcosis code, no more than 30 calendar days apart. The one-inpatient/two-noninpatient ascertainment structure follows established Medicare claims methods7,8; the 30-day interval is prespecified for this study.
The confirmation date is when the criterion is met. The index date is the earliest cryptococcosis diagnosis claim belonging to the qualifying episode, bounded to 30 days before confirmation. Do not mistake confirmation date for first observed diagnosis. Earlier isolated codes are characterized separately and subject to the uniform prior-history exclusion below; they do not automatically reset index to an arbitrarily earlier date.
Exclude an otherwise qualifying candidate index if an earlier cryptococcosis diagnosis is observed in the uniformly observable days −365 through −1 outside the 30-day qualifying episode. This exclusion also applies to pretransplant codes within that same uniformly observed period. Do not use extra years of uneven historical observation to exclude some patients but not others. The resulting case is a first observed qualifying diagnosis after a uniform lookback, not proven incident infection. The fixed 365-day period is a prespecified study choice: independent claims-methods literature demonstrates that washout length changes cohort classification9, but does not validate 365 days for cryptococcosis.
Keep the single-claim and other alternate case definitions for sensitivity analyses. Final clinical code lists will be available with the study materials.

4. Eligibility and transplant chronology
Include USRDS patients with a kidney transplant preceding the cryptococcosis index date (strictly earlier than day 0). Allow early post-transplant cases, retransplant recipients, and recipients with failed grafts or return to dialysis.
Require uninterrupted Medicare FFS primary Parts A and B (MPAB) coverage for each day −365 through day 0. Exclude Medicare Advantage, secondary, other-payer and uncovered intervals. Broader primary FFS (MPAB or MPO) eligibility is a sensitivity analysis. USRDS recommends Medicare primary for claims analyses and distinguishes MPAB from MPO; this study deliberately selects stricter MPAB for the primary cohort5. The uniform observation period establishes recorded history, not clinical absence.
Use the most recent kidney transplant preceding index to define time since transplant, transplant characteristics and center. For qualifying missed opportunities, encounters after any first kidney transplant can contribute, including before retransplantation. Do not count encounters before the first kidney transplant. For recent transplants, report the truncated post-transplant opportunity window; do not infer a full 90-day post-transplant observation window.
Graft status at index is based on reported transplant follow-up/graft-failure dates, not dialysis claims alone. Include graft failure in the primary cohort and restrict to functioning grafts in sensitivity analysis.
Residence ZIP and center linkage refer to the index date and relevant transplant episode. Missing geography does not exclude patients from primary proportions or mortality analyses.

A diagnosis category is newly recorded if no diagnosis in that category was documented during days −365 to −91. Distinct codes within the same category are not new. This does not establish symptom onset. Relevant diagnostic procedures need not be new.
Exclude personal-history diagnosis codes from opportunity categories. Use clinically reviewed, era-appropriate exact/prefix coding rules; ICD conversion crosswalks alone do not establish equivalence. Source literature guides phenotype development3; historical code-system and mapping guidance requires review of the corresponding code sets10.

6. Encounter-based opportunity ascertainment
The counting unit is a distinct clinical encounter (inpatient stay, outpatient institutional visit, or PS encounter independent of a stay), not claim lines. PS services during a hospitalization belong to the corresponding stay; multiple claims cannot manufacture distinct confirmation encounters or opportunities.
A qualifying encounter after first transplant and during the selected window contributes when it carries (a) a relevant diagnosis category newly recorded relative to the fixed prior-history period, or (b) a qualifying diagnostic procedure. Encounters meeting both pathways count once in the combined count but can contribute to multiple categories.
Exclude the entire index-spanning inpatient stay, including associated PS services, from the primary opportunity count. For documented direct transfers, recognize the continuous hospitalization while preserving constituent stays; an earlier transferring hospitalization of at least seven prediagnosis days may qualify under the transfer rule3. Describe prolonged prediagnosis index stays separately. Do not automatically merge a hospitalization after an outpatient index solely because it occurred within a fixed number of days.
Report patient-level proportions with explicit patient denominators, distinct qualifying encounters per patient (including zero), clinical categories, and time from the earliest qualifying encounter to index. Do not label elapsed time a measured diagnostic delay.
As descriptive context, plot weekly rates of encounters containing relevant diagnosis-category codes across days −365 to −1, irrespective of newness, overall and by neurologic, respiratory and infectious group. Do not fit a formal expected-rate comparison or infer a diagnostic threshold from the plot. This descriptive plot is a study-specific addition.

7. Covariates and baseline utilization
Prespecified mortality covariates: age at index, sex, time since most recent transplant, calendar year, diabetes, HIV, chronic liver disease, and malignancy.
Document a comorbidity during days −365 through −91 using one inpatient diagnosis or two distinct noninpatient encounters with relevant diagnoses, consistent with the general claims-ascertainment approach7. Otherwise classify it as not documented, not clinically absent. Report unknown status separately where ascertainment is impossible.
Describe distinct baseline inpatient stays and noninpatient encounters by missed-opportunity status, rurality and distance. Do not adjust mortality or primary geographic models for baseline utilization.

8. Mortality analyses
Follow from index to death, the administrative mortality ascertainment cutoff or the chosen horizon, whichever occurs first. Retain late-index cases and administratively censor them; do not require potential completion of each horizon. Report numbers at risk and follow-up completeness.
Report Kaplan–Meier absolute mortality estimates (30, 90 and 365 days) by opportunity status, with 95% confidence intervals. Use a conventional Cox model at 90 days as the preferred adjusted model when estimable. Prespecify penalized Cox regression for unstable sparse-event estimation11 and a simpler reduced model if needed. Do not select model terms based on statistical significance or the observed exposure effect. Weighting remains a separate exploratory approach, not an automatic solution to sparse events or disclosure risk.
Unresolved protocol dependency: objective feasibility thresholds and the precise hierarchy/covariate specification for sparse-comorbidity aggregation, penalization and reduced models must be settled in a tracked issue before exposure–mortality associations are examined. This draft does not claim that those criteria have been finalized.
Assess proportional hazards, influential observations and functional form. Interpret estimates as associations, subject to selection, surveillance and residual confounding.

9. Geographic secondary analyses
Residence is measured by ZIP code at index. Use period-appropriate ZIP-based RUCA primary codes 1–3 (urban/metropolitan) and 4–10 (rural/nonmetropolitan), using the USDA classification12, and straight-line miles from residential ZIP centroid to the most recent transplant center. Model distance continuously and report prevalence ratios per 50 miles, checking nonlinearity. Distance is not measured travel time.
Fit separate modified Poisson models with robust standard errors13 for rurality and distance, respectively, adjusting for the prespecified clinical covariates. Use separate complete-case cohorts for each geographic model; report denominators, exclusions and missingness. Do not adjust for baseline utilization; describe utilization by geography.

10. Sensitivity, limitations, reproducibility and disclosure
Prespecified sensitivities include nested 30-/60-day opportunity windows; single cryptococcosis claim; inpatient-only case ascertainment; first/principal listed cryptococcosis diagnosis; functioning graft only; broader MPAB plus MPO coverage; ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM eras separately. Report the effect of each sensitivity definition on the denominator and observation period.
Primary study size is determined by eligible claims and deaths; do not assert formally powered contrasts. Report complete-case exclusions for models, without imputing unobserved diagnoses as negative clinical findings.
Public code and code lists may be shared, but restricted patient-level data may not. Reports must suppress counts 1–10 and values derivable from complementary tables, figures or text, subject to the governing DUA. Weighted/adjusted estimates do not automatically eliminate disclosure risks. Report software and relevant package versions.
